external_dependencies.note: manifest declares no external_dependencies, but models/certificate.py and models/key.py import the 'cryptography' package (x509, hazmat.primitives) at module top level; tools/certificate_adapter.py imports pyOpenSSL (OpenSSL.crypto), requests and urllib3 — these are de-facto hard runtime dependencies not surfaced by the manifest.

security.detail: Both ACLs (certificate.certificate, certificate.key) grant full CRUD only to base.group_system (Settings/admin). Two ir.rule record rules enforce multi-company isolation via company_id parent_of company_ids on both models.

behavioral_notes.observation: The certificate.certificate record stores raw uploaded bytes (content: Binary) and parses them with the cryptography library, trying DER (x509.load_der_x509_certificate), then PKCS12 (pkcs12.load_key_and_certificates with the pkcs12_password), then PEM (x509.load_pem_x509_certificate). On success it derives and STORES content_format, a normalized pem_certificate, subject_common_name (from the COMMON_NAME OID), serial_number, and the validity window date_start/date_end read from the X.509 not_valid_before/not_valid_after (with a parse_version guard: cryptography <42.0.0 uses naive not_valid_before, >=42.0.0 uses not_valid_*_utc stripped to naive). On failure it sets loading_error. is_valid is a separate compute (date_start<=now<=date_end and no loading_error) with a matching _search_is_valid. These business attributes are produced entirely by reading the certificate bytes — invisible to ORM field metadata.

When a PKCS12 bundle is uploaded, _compute_private_key decodes the password-protected file, extracts the embedded private key, re-serializes it to unencrypted PKCS8 PEM, and CREATES (or de-duplicates against existing ir.attachment-stored content per company) a certificate.key record, linking it via private_key_id. So uploading one .p12 file silently spawns a second model record (the private key). The @api.constrains _constrains_certificate_key_compatibility then re-loads both and uses constant_time.bytes_eq to assert the certificate's public key matches the linked private/public key, raising ValidationError on mismatch. Cross-model side-effect + crypto consistency check not derivable from metadata.

certificate.key holds raw key bytes (content) plus an optional password and, via _compute_pem_key, attempts load_der/pem_private_key then load_der/pem_public_key to classify the key (public flag) and store a normalized pem_key (private keys re-encrypted with BestAvailableEncryption when a password is set, else NoEncryption). _sign loads the PEM private key (decrypting with the stored password) and dispatches by key type — EC -> ECDSA, RSA -> PKCS1v15, Ed25519 -> raw — over SHA1/SHA256, returning formatted signature bytes; _verify mirrors this with public keys; _decrypt handles RSA-OAEP. The model is a private-key vault that performs the actual cryptographic operations in-process.

certificate.certificate._sign is the public signing entry point used by document/e-invoice signing callers: it guards on is_valid (raising UserError if expired/invalid) and on the presence of private_key_id, then delegates to private_key_id._sign. Helper getters (_get_der_certificate_bytes, _get_fingerprint_bytes sha1/sha256, _get_signature_bytes, _get_public_key_bytes, _get_public_key_numbers_bytes) expose the certificate's DER/fingerprint/public-key material for embedding in signed XML/PDF. certificate.key also offers @api.model generators _generate_ec_private_key (SECP256R1), _generate_rsa_private_key (exp 65537/3, key_size>=512), and _generate_ed25519_private_key, each creating a certificate.key with a freshly generated, optionally password-encrypted PKCS8 key. These are the security primitives other modules (e.g. localized e-invoicing) consume.

The whole module is a thin ORM wrapper over the Python 'cryptography' package: certificate.py and key.py import cryptography.x509 and cryptography.hazmat.primitives (serialization, hashes, asymmetric ec/rsa/ed25519/padding, constant_time, pkcs12) at import time, and a runtime parse_version check against cryptography>=42.0.0 changes how validity dates are read. tools/certificate_adapter.py additionally imports pyOpenSSL (OpenSSL.crypto load_certificate/load_privatekey), requests and urllib3 to build a CertificateAdapter (requests.adapters.HTTPAdapter) that performs mutual-TLS using in-memory certificate.certificate / certificate.key records instead of on-disk files. None of these are declared in the manifest's external_dependencies.

certificate ships zero frontend: 0 JS files, 0 XML/OWL templates, 0 registry adds, 0 patches, 0 services, no asset bundles. All UI is plain backend form/list/search views (2 each) plus a res.config.settings extension; it is a pure server-side cryptographic utility with no client-side code.

it_architecture.application: certificate (server-side X.509 certificate & private-key vault and signing/crypto utility)
software_services: (no HTTP routes; exposes in-process ORM service methods: certificate.certificate._sign, _get_der_certificate_bytes, _get_fingerprint_bytes, _get_signature_bytes, _get_public_key_bytes, _get_public_key_numbers_bytes; certificate.key._sign/_verify/_decrypt and _generate_ec/rsa/ed25519_private_key)
tools.CertificateAdapter: a requests HTTPAdapter providing mutual-TLS from in-memory certificate records (outbound transport helper, no inbound route)
information_flows: uses cryptography (x509/hazmat) to parse uploaded cert/key bytes into stored business attributes (subject, serial, validity, pem)
side-effect: uploading a PKCS12 bundle creates a derived certificate.key (private key) record
consumed by downstream signing modules (e-invoicing / document signing localizations) via _sign and certificate/key byte getters
tools.CertificateAdapter injects in-memory cert+key into pyOpenSSL/urllib3 for outbound mutual-TLS HTTPS

capabilities: Store & Normalize Digital Certificates (DER/PEM/PKCS12 -> stored PEM + parsed metadata)
Manage Cryptographic Key Pairs (private/public key vault: certificate.key)
Generate Asymmetric Keys (EC SECP256R1, RSA, Ed25519)
Validate Certificate Lifecycle (validity window, cert/key compatibility check)
Provide Mutual-TLS Transport from In-Memory Certificates (CertificateAdapter)
value_streams: Upload-to-Usable-Credential: upload cert/key bytes -> cryptography parses & validates -> stored normalized PEM + validity + linked key -> credential ready for signing
Sign-on-Demand: caller invokes certificate._sign(message) -> validity & private-key guard -> key._sign dispatch by algorithm -> signature bytes returned to the document/e-invoice module
organization: base.group_system (Settings/admin) — the only group granted access to both models (no module-specific security groups defined)
policies: ACL: full CRUD on certificate.certificate and certificate.key restricted to base.group_system
ir.rule: multi-company isolation on both models (company_id = False OR company_id parent_of company_ids)
@api.constrains: certificate must load successfully (else ValidationError) and certificate/key public material must match (constant_time compare)
_sign refuses to sign with an invalid/expired certificate or without a linked private key
stakeholders: Downstream e-invoicing / document-signing localization modules (programmatic consumers)
External TLS endpoints requiring client-certificate authentication
metrics: is_valid / loading_error as operational health indicators per certificate (no reports or KPI dashboards shipped)

classification.rationale: By Stabell & Fjeldstad, certificate is a pure 'support' value model: it is firm IT/security infrastructure (a PKI credential vault plus signing/crypto primitives) with no business object, document flow or transaction of its own — it owns only certificate.certificate and certificate.key, has no routes, no reports, no product, and is restricted to base.group_system. It creates no customer value directly; it is consumed by primary/support activities (e-invoicing, document signing, mutual-TLS) as a technology-development/infrastructure utility. APQC 8.0 'Manage Information Technology' is the correct category because the module's whole purpose is cryptographic key and certificate management — i.e. IT security administration (key generation, secure key storage, certificate lifecycle, digital signing) which sits under 8.0 'Manage IT' (IT security, privacy and data protection / manage IT infrastructure). It was weighed against 11.0 'Manage Enterprise Risk, Compliance, Remediation, and Resiliency': although digital signatures serve legal/compliance (e-invoice authenticity, non-repudiation), this module supplies only the technical cryptographic mechanism, not the governance, risk assessment, audit or compliance process itself — that compliance use lives in the consuming localization modules. The dominant character here is cryptographic key/certificate management infrastructure, so 8.0 is chosen with 11.0 noted as the secondary (downstream) concern.

standard_capabilities: upload and store X.509 certificates in DER, PEM or PKCS12, auto-detecting format
auto-extract subject common name, serial number and validity dates from certificate bytes
auto-derive and link the private key from an uploaded PKCS12 bundle
store and classify private/public keys, password-protected, per company
generate EC (SECP256R1), RSA and Ed25519 key pairs
sign (ECDSA/RSA/Ed25519, SHA1/SHA256), verify, and RSA-OAEP decrypt
certificate/key compatibility and validity enforcement via constraints
mutual-TLS HTTP transport from in-memory certificates (CertificateAdapter)
typical_fits: credential store for country-specific e-invoicing / e-signature localizations reused unchanged
admin-only, multi-company certificate management out of the box
programmatic signing API (_sign) for any module needing X.509 signatures
common_gaps: no UI/workflow for certificate expiry alerts or rotation reminders (only the is_valid flag)
limited curve/algorithm coverage (EC fixed to SECP256R1; SHA1/SHA256 only)
no HSM / external key-store integration; private keys stored in the database
no certificate enrollment / CA issuance flow (import-only)
manifest omits the cryptography/pyOpenSSL external dependencies
drive_hints: odoo shell: env['certificate.key']._generate_rsa_private_key(env.company, name='demo_rsa')  # generate a key pair
odoo shell: k = env['certificate.key']._generate_ec_private_key(env.company); k._sign('hello')  # sign a message
odoo shell: c = env['certificate.certificate'].browse(id); (c.subject_common_name, c.date_end, c.is_valid)  # parsed cert metadata

open_questions: Which downstream modules call certificate.certificate._sign (e-invoicing localizations vs document signing) and with what hashing algorithms — not visible from this module alone.
Whether private keys stored in the database (Binary/ir.attachment) meet the deployment's key-protection / compliance requirements, given no HSM integration.
Whether CertificateAdapter is actually wired into a live outbound request flow in this codebase or only provided as a helper.
